lecture_beats.subject: QED and QCD are introduced as two gauge theories already encountered.
The lecture promises a minimal physical definition rather than the full mathematics of gauge symmetry.
Maxwell electromagnetism is selected as the simplest gauge theory.
The electromagnetic field has three electric and three magnetic components.
Those six field components can be encoded by a four-vector potential.
The time component is identified with electrostatic potential.
Spatial derivatives of the scalar potential give the electric field.
The magnetic field is the curl of the vector potential.
Field and potential descriptions are equivalent.
Maxwell equations produce electromagnetic waves.
A wave has a propagation direction and polarization.
Electric and magnetic fields oscillate as the wave moves.
Electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular and equal in suitable units.
The electric-field direction specifies linear polarization.
Electromagnetic fields have charges and currents as sources.
A point charge produces a radial electric field.
Electric field lines can end only on charges.
The radial field decreases as inverse distance squared.
A fixed number of field lines crosses every surrounding sphere.
The flux statement is identified as Gauss's law.
Gauss's law has the strong consequence of charge conservation.
Instant disappearance of a Coulomb field would violate causality.
The flux-and-source picture is called the essence of gauge theory.
Gauge fields are Maxwell-like electric-like and magnetic-like fields.
A weakly coupled gauge field propagates like a polarized light wave.
Every gauge field has sources, though the source need not be electric charge.
Baryon number is proposed as a mathematically possible but unphysical gauge source.
Protons and neutrons carry the same-sign baryon number.
A baryon gauge field would create Coulomb-like forces between nucleons.
Protons and antiprotons would attract through opposite baryon charge.
Nature shows no corresponding long-range baryon-number gauge field.
The classical wave description is translated into quantum field quanta.
A photon is pictured as a localized quantum carrying polarization.
Photon polarization can be rotated by optical elements.
The Coulomb field is roughly pictured through photon emission and absorption.
Electric charge conservation is tied to phase rotation of the charged field.
The discussion returns to the more complicated QCD gauge theory.
The gluon field is represented as a matrix A with two color indices.
The relevant color group is SU(3).
A quark field carries one red-green-blue color index.
A special-unitary matrix transforms the quark color vector.
Quarks form the three-dimensional fundamental or defining representation.
Antiquark fields are complex conjugates of quark fields.
The conjugate field transforms with the conjugate matrix.
Quarks and antiquarks carry the three and three-bar representations.
Audience asks how many matrices or generators SU(3) has.
The possibility of U(3) rather than SU(3) is acknowledged and postponed.
The two-index gluon field transforms like quark times antiquark.
Tracelessness removes the singlet and leaves eight gluons.
Gluons transform under color, unlike electrically neutral photons.
Electron, positron, and photon phase transformations are contrasted.
A gluon carries a color and an anticolor.
The gluons form the adjoint representation.
The lecture turns from representations to interaction vertices.
Other SU(N) gauge theories share the same pattern.
Fundamental objects and anti-objects carry one index of conjugate types.
Gauge bosons carry one fundamental and one antifundamental index.
SU(N) has N squared minus one generators and gauge bosons.
A quark changes color by emitting a gluon.
Color indices are followed continuously through each vertex.
Fundamental matter, gauge bosons, and index conservation summarize the interaction rule.
A colored gluon can itself emit another gluon.
The three-gluon color flow introduces an intermediate color index.
Gluon self-charge is identified as absent in electrodynamics.
Non-Abelian gluon dynamics is noted to be far more complicated than photon dynamics.
The confinement picture begins with a quark and antiquark joined by continuous flux.
Interacting field lines are pulled into flux tubes.
Flux-tube energy grows linearly with quark separation.
Maxwell-like fields, sources, Gauss law, conservation, and symmetry are summarized.
A coupling constant is added as the remaining gauge-theory ingredient.
Electric charge is the amplitude at a photon-emission vertex.
Stopping an electron in a cathode-ray tube supplies an operational picture.
Photon-emission probability is proportional to the square of charge.
The amplitude-probability distinction is emphasized.
In natural units electric charge is dimensionless.
Conventional four-pi factors define the fine-structure constant.
Alpha is approximately one over 137.
Roughly one out of 137 stopping events emits a photon in the illustrative picture.
Small emission probability makes electromagnetism perturbatively weak.
Orders of magnitude are introduced to compare electromagnetic, strong, and weak processes.
QCD is identified with the historically named strong interaction among hadrons.
Strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions are placed side by side.
Energy, distance, and time units are related.
Setting the speed of light to one equates units of time and distance.
Setting Planck's constant to one simplifies quantum units.
The Planck relation connects energy to frequency.
Frequency has units inverse to time.
Large energy corresponds to short time.
Distance likewise has inverse-energy units.
An inverse electronvolt is introduced as a distance unit.
Its order of magnitude is about ten to the minus seven meters.
An atomic diameter is about ten to the minus ten meters.
An inverse kiloelectronvolt is associated with atomic length.
The atomic light-crossing time is about ten to the minus eighteen seconds.
The electron orbital period is distinguished from the light-crossing time.
Weak electromagnetism makes the bound electron move slowly compared with light.
The atomic orbital time is estimated near ten to the minus sixteen seconds.
The radiative lifetime of an excited atom is introduced.
Small acceleration and small photon-emission probability give two suppressions.
An atomic decay time of nanosecond order is quoted.
Transit, orbital, and decay times form an alpha-controlled hierarchy.
Hadrons are compared with atoms made from quarks.
A typical hadron has diameter near ten to the minus fifteen meters.
Heavier constituents and stronger binding help explain the smaller scale.
The hadronic light-crossing time is about ten to the minus twenty-three seconds.
Quark orbital motion occurs on the same time scale.
Strong decays of excited hadrons also occur on that time scale.
The absence of a hierarchy implies a much larger strong coupling.
Audience asks whether relativity sets the minimum decay time.
Strong processes are described as nearly as fast as possible.
A representative QCD coupling near one fifth is quoted.
Audience asks the conventional name of the strong coupling.
Audience discusses alpha-QED and bare versus renormalized couplings.
The lecture turns to weak interactions.
Weak decay lifetimes exceed strong and often atomic lifetimes.
The neutron is chosen as the oldest weak-decay example.
Neutron beta decay products and a roughly twelve-minute lifetime are written.
A small available energy is identified as one partial explanation.
Approximate neutron, proton, and electron masses are compared.
Below threshold the neutron could not decay.
Near threshold, small phase space would slow decay.
Phase space is declared insufficient to explain twelve minutes.
Charged-pion decay provides a second weak example.
The charge-conjugate positive-pion channel is noted.
A nanosecond-order pion lifetime is quoted.
A corresponding muon channel is announced.
Pion decay has ample available energy, eliminating the threshold excuse.
Beta-ray terminology and the common weak physics are recalled.
Understanding weak decay requires introducing leptons.
The six quark flavors are arranged in paired columns.
Every flavor has red, blue, and green color copies.
Color SU(3) acts vertically among color rows.
The row-versus-column drawing convention is clarified.
Weak transformations act horizontally within flavor pairs.
Up-type and down-type families repeat their properties apart from mass.
The audience identifies SU(2) as the group acting on doublets.
Weak SU(2) is identified as a gauge symmetry with fields and bosons.
A fourth noncolored row is added to the table.
The fourth row is identified as leptons.
The electron is paired with the electron neutrino.
The muon is paired with the muon neutrino.
The tau is paired with the tau neutrino.
Neutrinos are neutral while charged leptons carry charge minus one.
Quark and lepton doublet members differ by one unit of charge.
A break is taken before introducing W bosons.
The lecture resumes by constructing a microscopic weak gauge theory.
Gauge-boson quantum numbers are modeled on particle-antiparticle pairs.
The construction is independent of color and begins with leptons.
Neutral particle-antiparticle combinations are acknowledged and postponed.
Electron plus electron-antineutrino quantum numbers are considered.
The charge-minus-one gauge boson is named W-minus.
Down plus anti-up has the same charge and weak quantum-number change.
The conjugate combinations define W-plus.
W bosons are assumed to be emitted and absorbed like other gauge bosons.
An electron changes to its neutrino by emitting W-minus.
A down quark changes to an up quark through the same boson.
The weak transition preserves the quark's color.
A strange quark can change to a charm quark.
One horizontal symmetry unifies all charged-current transitions.
W-plus and W-minus are antiparticles and diagrams can be reversed.
Audience asks why one W species mediates all families.
Audience asks whether arrows and lines may be flipped.
Audience clarifies that quark labels denote W quantum numbers, not constituents.
Audience combines a lepton entrance channel with a quark exit channel.
The pion decay derivation begins.
Pi-minus is identified as down plus anti-up.
The valence pair annihilates into W-minus.
W-minus produces an electron and electron antineutrino.
The outgoing antineutrino flavor is fixed by the charged lepton.
The muon and muon-antineutrino channel is added.
Audience asks about the diagram's horizontal time convention.
The muon channel is identified as the dominant charged-pion decay.
Audience asks whether the reaction can be read in reverse.
Three SU(2) generators imply a third neutral gauge boson.
Audience asks whether weak or strong interactions were historically suspected first.
Becquerel radioactivity is divided into alpha, beta, and gamma processes.
Audience asks how energy conservation works through the intermediate W.
The short-lived off-shell intermediate-state argument is given.
The pion rest mass is estimated near 140 MeV.
Muon and neutrino rest masses are compared.
Excess rest energy becomes final-state kinetic energy.
Back-to-back momenta conserve momentum in the pion rest frame.
Neutron decay is deferred briefly in favor of the simpler muon decay.
A muon emits W-minus and becomes a muon neutrino.
The virtual W produces an electron and electron antineutrino.
Muon decay is kinematically allowed and observed.
The process is classified as purely leptonic.
Audience confirms the electron antineutrino in the final state.
The displayed channel is identified as the muon's decay.
Muon instability and electron stability follow from their mass ordering.
The tau can decay through analogous lepton channels.
Both muon vertices repeat the same doublet-changing component.
The discussion returns to neutron beta decay.
Audience asks whether accelerators effectively increase particle mass.
A neutron is decomposed as two down quarks and one up quark.
Up-to-down conversion would produce a too-heavy three-down state.
One down quark instead converts to an up quark and emits W-minus.
The resulting up-up-down baryon is a proton.
The W produces the electron and electron antineutrino.
Audience asks whether a neutron could produce a muon channel.
Additional collision energy would make a related muon-producing process possible.
The lecture closes by returning to the puzzle of slow weak rates.
An extremely tiny weak coupling is proposed as a possible explanation.
The weak coupling is stated to be comparable to the electromagnetic coupling.
Audience confirms that symmetry means invariance of the Lagrangian.
